title: The impact of honeybee abundance on wild bees and hoverfly biodiversity in Scottish oilseed rape fields
content:
Abstract
Managed honeybees can negatively affect wild pollinators. However, reported impacts are context-dependent, and little is known about effects on non-bee pollinators. We hypothesized that (a) increasing honeybee abundance would decrease wild pollinator biodiversity, with the magnitude and direction of these effects varying among taxonomic groups, (b) temporal partitioning of foraging activity may enable some groups to avoid honeybees, and (c) semi-natural habitat (SNH) cover and hedgerows may moderate the associations between managed honeybees and wild pollinators. In spring 2024 and 2025, we surveyed honeybees, wild bees, and hoverflies along field and hedgerow transects at 12 sites with a gradient in the number of honeybee hives. Using generalized and linear mixed models, we tested whether honeybee abundance influenced wild pollinator abundance, richness, and diversity. We also tested whether SNH cover and hedgerows moderated these associations. We detected a positive overall association between standardized honeybee abundance and wild pollinator abundance, but only at sites with low SNH cover. Hoverfly abundance declined significantly as honeybee abundance increased. Habitat (field versus hedgerow) and sampling time did not substantially alter these patterns. However, increasing SNH cover was associated with increasing wild pollinator diversity, while hedgerows supported a higher average abundance of wild pollinators than oilseed rape fields. Our findings reveal taxon-specific responses to managed honeybee abundance, but SNH cover modifies some responses. Further research is needed to assess the long-term implications for hoverflies, as potential effects may affect ecosystem function. These findings highlight the potential importance of maintaining SNH within agricultural landscapes.
